# Authoring notes: Real Analysis, Sequences & Modes of Convergence

Canonical topic ID: `real-analysis-sequences-modes-of-convergence`

## 2026-09-11 — Use Fourier jump neighborhoods to distinguish convergence claims

- Status: open; merge with the existing finite Taylor and quantifier-order entries below.
- Origin: sections 3–5 of `complex-numbers-fourier-laplace-transforms`, [design record](../COMPLEX-FOURIER-LAPLACE-LESSON-DESIGN.md). This origin is still design-only; no completed Fourier implementation or general proof is claimed.
- Existing coverage and ownership: the current analysis brief owns pointwise/uniform convergence and invalid interchange. The Fourier design proposes finite orthogonal projection, a square-wave partial sum, piecewise-smooth midpoint convergence and a carefully bounded continuous-transform bridge. General convergence modes and operation interchange belong here.
- Proposed benefit and example: contrast a fixed point away from a square-wave jump with a point moving toward the jump as the cutoff grows. Small mean-square error does not imply a small supremum error. State which function values are defined at the jump and distinguish that point from an entire shrinking neighborhood. Link this to the existing moving-spike and witness-dependency explanations rather than creating an unrelated metaphor.
- Boundaries: a sampled finite maximum is not a proof of uniform convergence or its failure; use an analytical witness or theorem. Fourier coefficient decay does not by itself authorize termwise differentiation without suitable convergence and regularity assumptions. The full Plancherel/density extension remains a separate advanced result, not a prerequisite inferred from a finite energy identity.
- Evidence: [Lebl's piecewise-smooth Fourier convergence theorem](https://www.jirka.org/diffyqs/html/moreonfourier_section.html), especially section 4.3.2, was read on 11 September 2026. The exact scaled-neighborhood/asymptotic calculation remains an implementation proof obligation for the Fourier origin and a reassessment obligation here.
- Resolution: receiving author should select an appropriate changed family and state its hypotheses; retain the local distinction from formal generating functions already mentioned below. No analysis body or shared prerequisite edge was changed.

## 2026-09-11 — Carry finite Taylor control into series and interchange theory

- Status: open; assessed during Calculus47 authoring.
- Origin: section10 of `single-variable-calculus-limits-derivatives-integrals` and [its design](../SINGLE-VARIABLE-CALCULUS-LESSON-DESIGN.md).
- Existing local coverage: a finite Taylor polynomial with an integral remainder under C^(n+1) assumptions; the derivative-bound estimate; a factorial-ratio argument showing exp's remainder vanishes at fixed x; and the log(1+x) series derived from a finite geometric identity. The log proof distinguishes |x|<1, a separately justified x=1 endpoint, divergence at x=−1 and term failure outside radius1. It does not provide general series convergence or termwise-operation theorems.
- Best owner and learning benefit: Real Analysis already owns sequences, convergence modes and invalid limit interchange. Develop series as limits of partial sums, the radius/endpoint distinction, and why pointwise convergence alone does not allow differentiating or integrating a series. Connect to the existing quantifier-order notes rather than adding an isolated formula table.
- Proposed treatment: a changed family or power series with separate endpoint behavior; sufficient uniform-convergence conditions for integration on a compact interval, and properly qualified derivative-series convergence conditions. Explain whether convergence of the derivatives plus one base value is needed. Show a counterexample before the valid theorem and test a changed set/domain. Do not assert that smooth functions necessarily equal their Taylor series.
- Sources actually checked: OpenStax Calculus2 §6.3 theorem6.7/remainder and §6.4 nonelementary Gaussian integral. Their selected finite results support the origin; general power-series and interchange claims require the destination's own primary-source investigation.
- Prerequisites and limits: elementary sequences, limits and the Calculus derivative/integral core; do not create a circular dependency through older advanced mathematics topics. Formal generating functions in Counting46 are algebraic coefficient objects and require a separate explicit transition before any analytic convergence claim.
- Resolution: receiving author must include, adapt or justify a different owner, recording the actual explanation and verification. No Real Analysis body was created by this note.

## 2026-09-11 — Translate finite witness order into an analysis dependency

- Status: open; coordinate with the existing measure-theory note below.
- Origin: Math44 Sets, Logic, Relations & Proof Techniques section4 and its [design](../SETS-LOGIC-LESSON-DESIGN.md).
- Existing foundation: a job/reviewer board distinguishes one reviewer chosen separately for every job from a single reviewer fixed before the job is known. Negation pushes through quantifiers one at a time; exact empty-domain behavior is taught locally. The written integer example chooses m=n+1 after n and refutes one integer greater than every integer.
- Destination rationale: this lesson explicitly owns pointwise/uniform convergence and epsilon definitions. When it is implemented, use that witness-dependency habit to distinguish an eventual index allowed to depend on x and ε from one depending on ε alone across all x. Introduce sequences, distance, limits and the epsilon meaning locally before the comparison; do not force students to infer an analytic theorem from the finite staffing metaphor.
- Proposed benefit: write the dependency of N explicitly, then choose a changed function family exposing the invalid common-witness inference. The prior measure note already suggests fixed-point versus moving-spike counterexamples; combine these rather than create disconnected metaphors.
- Accuracy boundary: no pointwise/uniform convergence theorem was proved in Sets44. Any integral/limit interchange needs its actual measure/continuity/boundedness hypotheses. This note is a reasoned handoff, not an imported proof or a prerequisite cycle.
- Resolution: receiving author must assess and record its adopted explanation, exact counterexample and independent verification; no destination body changed here.

## 2026-09-10 — Connect quantifier order to the measure lesson's fixed-point and moving-spike examples

- Status: open
- Origin: [Measure Theory design](../MEASURE-THEORY-PROBABILITY-SPACES-DESIGN.md), section 6 of `measure-theory-probability-spaces`.
- Destination and ownership rationale: exact topic-plan command confirms a planned analysis topic with pointwise/uniform convergence and invalid interchange as explicit outcomes. This is the correct home for the epsilon/N quantifier comparison; keep advanced probability convergence criteria in a clearly optional bridge rather than making measure theory a prerequisite of the introductory core.
- Idea and learning benefit: distinguish one fixed x from the changing choice x=1/(2n). In f_n=n·1_(0,1/n), every fixed point eventually sees zero, although the integral remains one and the supremum does not decrease. Compare x^n on [0,1], which has an exceptional limit value at 1, with uniform convergence on [0,r] for fixed r<1. Tie uniform convergence on a finite-measure domain to |∫f_n−∫f|≤μ(domain) sup|f_n−f|, explaining why that argument needs finite measure.
- Existing coverage: the destination brief (inspected 10 September) already plans pointwise versus uniform convergence and a limit-integral counterexample. The current Measure Theory lesson supplies MCT, Fatou, DCT and the exact fixed-point/integral comparison, but does not teach a complete map of modes of convergence or uniform integrability.
- Proposed treatment: use changed functions and explicit quantifier order in the core; link back to the Measure Theory counterexample only for readers with that context. Assess an optional uniform-integrability bridge after probability convergence has been introduced. Do not equate bounded L1 norms with uniform integrability or claim it follows from one fixed sample plot.
- Evidence: [Axler's author-hosted book](https://measure.axler.net/MIRA.pdf), scoped sections 3.9/3.11 and 3.31 inspected for the measure lesson; finite teaching models independently verified. The stronger optional uniform-integrability theorem has not been researched in this authoring scope and requires its own primary-source/hypothesis review.
- Prerequisites and boundaries: elementary sequences and epsilon definitions for the core; measurable random variables and probability convergence for any optional uniform-integrability statement. No prerequisite cycle should be introduced merely to cross-link an application.
- Resolution: receiving author should merge with the already planned outcomes and decide whether the optional probability branch helps this topic or should be routed to a stochastic-process topic. No destination body or title changed.
- Implementation/verification links: origin `scripts/verify-measure-theory.mjs`, `scratch/measure-theory-verification/native-results.json`, and [Measure Theory verification](../MEASURE-THEORY-PROBABILITY-SPACES-VERIFICATION.md).

## 2026-09-10 — Establish a teaching owner for bit manipulation in interview preparation

- Status: open
- Origin: [DSA practice standard and evolving coverage map](../DSA-PRACTICE-STANDARD.md), prepared while adding practice to the first five DSA lessons.
- Proposed destination and alternatives: find an existing programming/DSA owner before proposing a new topic. A scoped search of track definitions and curriculum source for bitwise, bit manipulation, bitmask and XOR found incidental numerical-reproducibility mentions, not an explicit DSA teaching home. This does not prove that no relevant sentence exists elsewhere.
- Idea and learning benefit: a future interview-preparation route should teach masks as sets, bitwise versus boolean operations, width/sign and shift contracts, and the reasoning behind useful XOR identities before asking learners to memorize bit tricks. Determine which mechanisms already belong to a foundation lesson and which need a DSA extension.
- Existing coverage: unresolved in this narrow title/brief search. The first five DSA practice sets do not establish coverage of this family, and the current three-lesson request is not a full-catalogue audit.

Preserve stable IDs and module order. Do not insert an unexplained hard problem into the present foundation sets merely to increase breadth.
- Prerequisites and boundaries: integer representation, boolean logic, sets, language-specific bit/shift semantics; distinguish Python's integer behavior from fixed-width machine integers. API/version details must be researched before authoring.
- Evidence: the local curriculum search and the explicitly partial practice coverage map; no new technical implementation claim or source endorsement is made by this note.
- Resolution: unassigned; no topic added and no existing lesson rewritten by this discovery.
